analysis.one_liner: Banned unlimited soft money in politics, tightened campaign disclosure, and created a commission to fix election administration.
analysis.headline: The Senate's broad campaign finance and election reform bill was referred to the Rules and Administration Committee on the day it was introduced in January 2001 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have banned national political parties from raising or spending unlimited 'soft money' — money not subject to federal contribution limits — and barred federal candidates from soliciting it. It tightened disclosure of who pays for campaign ads, strengthened the ban on foreign money, raised penalties for violations, limited incumbents' use of taxpayer-funded mass mailings before elections, and set up a commission and federal grant program to help states fix voting machines, ballots, and polling place access. It also guaranteed that servicemembers stationed away from home keep their voting residency.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters who want to know who is paying for political ads, candidates who cannot tap big soft-money donors, and citizens affected by outdated voting equipment or confusing ballots. Military voters away from their home states would gain a clear guarantee they can vote absentee in state and local elections.

how_it_helps.text: Bars national party committees from soliciting, receiving, or spending any money not subject to federal contribution limits and reporting rules, and blocks state and local party committees from using such money for federal election activity like voter registration and get-out-the-vote drives.

Requires anyone making independent TV or radio ads that name a candidate within 60 days of an election to report the spending within 24-48 hours, and requires a clearly stated 'who paid for this' disclosure on campaign ads.
Strengthens the foreign-money ban, removes the 'willful blindness' defense, and raises the criminal penalty for foreign contributions to up to 10 years in prison and a $1 million fine.

Establishes a Commission on Voting Rights and Procedures to study voting technology, ballot design, polling place access, and voter education, with federal matching grants to states to implement its recommendations.

Prohibits fundraising on federal property, bars selling access to the White House or Air Force One, requires parties to reimburse the government at fair market value for political use of Air Force One, and publishes the names of non-government passengers on presidential aircraft.
Guarantees that servicemembers absent under military orders do not lose their voting residency, and requires states to let uniformed services members vote absentee in state and local elections.

analysis.who_pays: National party committees and the large donors, corporations, and unions that gave unlimited soft money would lose that channel, which is why both parties' national committees fought similar bans. Labor unions would face new requirements to notify nonmember employees and refund the share of their fees spent on politics. Incumbent lawmakers would lose the ability to send taxpayer-funded mass mailings in the 180 days before a general election.
analysis.who_pays_short: Party committees, big soft-money donors, unions

drawbacks.text: The bill raised the individual aggregate contribution limit from $25,000 to $30,000 and created a new $10,000 annual limit for state party committees, which critics of similar bills said partly offset the soft-money ban by steering more large hard money through the parties.

It codifies the Supreme Court's Beck decision into the National Labor Relations Act, requiring unions to give annual notice to nonmember fee-payers and refund the portion of their payments that goes to politics unrelated to collective bargaining — a cost and compliance burden on unions that supporters of labor law viewed as unnecessary.

The express advocacy definition treats any broadcast ad referring to a clearly identified candidate within 60 days of an election as campaign advocacy subject to federal limits and disclosure, a breadth that raises First Amendment concerns about sweeping issue discussion into campaign rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: the soft-money ban and disclosure rules would cut off the largest unregulated money channel in federal politics and let voters see who pays for ads, in exchange for somewhat higher hard-money limits and a new administrative burden on unions. The election-administration and military voting provisions address problems exposed by the 2000 election with little downside beyond cost. On balance the benefits to ordinary voters outweigh the acknowledged trade-offs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee on the day it was introduced, never reported out, and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Daschle introduced the Federal Elections Reform Act of 2001 on January 22, 2001, joined by 19 Democratic colleagues including Dodd, Lieberman, Kennedy, Biden, Boxer, and Clinton.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration the same day.
Twenty Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
The full action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee report, no floor vote — through the end of the 107th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: National party committees and large soft-money donors kept that unregulated funding channel through the 2002 elections, and incumbents kept their existing fundraising and franking practices. Broader campaign finance reform did reach law in this same Congress through the separate McCain-Feingold bill (the 2002 Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act), but this broader package — with its election-administration grants and voting-rights commission — never advanced at all.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Party committees and big soft-money donors

for.name: Tom Daschle
for.role: Senate Democratic Leader; later Senate Majority Leader
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on the Senate floor on January 22, 2001.

against.name: Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and never reported it out, held no markup, and allowed it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.role: Chair, Senate Rules and Administration Committee (January-June 2001)
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee to which the bill was referred during the first half of 2001, when no action was taken; he was the Senate's best-known opponent of campaign finance limits.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 supporters — the sponsor and 20 cosponsors — were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a vote in a Senate that Republicans controlled for its first months and Democrats controlled thereafter.

industries.industry: National political parties and large soft-money donors
industries.note: The bill's centerpiece bans national parties from soliciting, receiving, or spending money outside federal limits and blocks parties from routing soft money to tax-exempt groups. This closes the channel that let corporations, unions, and wealthy donors give six- and seven-figure sums beyond ordinary limits.

The bill writes the Beck decision into law, requiring unions to notify nonmember fee-payers each year and refund the share of their payments spent on electioneering and lobbying unrelated to collective bargaining.

A federal grant program would fund states to upgrade voting systems, ballot design, and polling place access, creating demand for election equipment and services that serves voters' interest in accurate, accessible elections.
